title: When It Rains, Sewage Can Go Straight Into the River #shorts
summary: About 700 US communities have combined sewers, where sewage and stormwater share pipes; in a hard rain, relief outlets spill the mix into rivers untreated or partly treated (EPA). Canada reported 134 million m3 of combined sewer overflows in 2023 (ECCC).
sources: There are approximately 700 communities in the United States that have combined sewer systems, mostly in the northeast and around the Great Lakes (US EPA, Where Combined Sewer Overflows Are Located, updated 4 May 2026): https://www.epa.gov/npdes/where-combined-sewer-overflows-are-located

In a combined sewer system, wastewater and stormwater flow through the same pipes; in wet weather the combined flow can overwhelm the system, and permitted outfalls act as relief points that discharge untreated or partially treated stormwater and wastewater into nearby waterbodies (US EPA, Combined Sewer Overflow Basics): https://epa.gov/npdes/combined-sewer-overflow-basics

Over 2013-2023 about 86% of Canada's population was served by municipal wastewater systems; in 2023, 215 million m3 of municipal wastewater was discharged with no treatment, including 134 million m3 from combined sewer overflows (Environment and Climate Change Canada, Canadian Environmental Sustainability Indicators: Municipal wastewater treatment, Sept 2025): https://www.canada.ca/content/dam/eccc/documents/pdf/cesindicators/municipal-wastewater-treatmenet/2025/municipal-wastewater-treatment-en.pdf

scenes.narration: In about {700|seven hundred} US communities, a hard rain sends sewage into the river.
Their sewers are combined. Toilets and storm drains share the same pipes.
In a storm, that's too much, so relief outlets spill it, untreated or partly treated.
In {2023|twenty twenty-three}, Canada reported {134 million|a hundred thirty-four million} cubic metres of it.
It's built in, on purpose. So when it pours, remember:
